deadline_report.summary: A-control: 1041 of 1299 cycles missed the 10 ms deadline (80.1%); worst response 49.1 ms, 99th percentile 46.7 ms, mean 24.41 ms. The misses form 130 run(s) of consecutive misses (longest 9); what started each run: waiting for a server's reply (message passing) (130).

result.summary: 1 finding(s); most likely: Priority inversion through message passing: rtdemo[21360661] waits on rtdemo[21372930] (high confidence). Kernel trace (1000 ms): 1 of 1 finding(s) confirmed step by step.

findings.title: Priority inversion through message passing: rtdemo[21360661] waits on rtdemo[21372930]
findings.explanation: rtdemo[21360661] 'A-control' (priority 30) waits for a reply from rtdemo[21372930] 'S-server', which serves it at priority 10, while rtdemo[21360661] 'B-worker' (priority 20) keeps the server's CPU. The reply cannot come until the middle-priority work stops, so the high-priority client waits for unrelated work. No mutex is involved.
evidence: In 16 of 23 snapshots rtdemo[21360661] 'A-control' (priority 30) was waiting on a message to process rtdemo[21372930] (REPLY 16), for up to 44 ms.

In 16 of those, the server's working thread rtdemo[21372930] 'S-server' ran at priority 10, below its client. On QNX a server thread that receives a message normally runs at the client's priority, so it was not inheriting it.
In 9 snapshot(s) a thread between the two priorities had the server's CPU: rtdemo[21360661] 'B-worker' at priority 20 (RUNNING).

The deadline report for A-control shows 1041 misses in 130 run(s) of consecutive misses; 130 of those runs started with a long wait for a server's reply (worst 47.4 ms from send to reply; the server's usual answer time is 4.0 ms).
could_not_determine: Snapshots are instants: 23 were taken, and qbridged reads processes one after another, so client and server are not read at exactly the same moment.

Why the server does not inherit the client's priority: qbridge cannot read a channel's flags. _NTO_CHF_FIXED_PRIORITY on the server's channel has this effect; so would a server that sets its own priority after receiving.
Which server thread received this client's message, if the server process has several working threads: the snapshot names the process, not the thread.
A worst case: finite runs cannot prove the deadline will always be met after a fix.
findings.suggested_fix: Let the server inherit its clients' priority, the QNX default: create its channel without _NTO_CHF_FIXED_PRIORITY (and do not lower the server thread's priority after MsgReceive). The server then works for a client at the client's priority, so a middle-priority thread can no longer delay the reply. If the server must keep a fixed priority, run it above the threads that compete for its CPU.

steps.claim: rtdemo[21360661] 'A-control' blocks waiting for a server (SEND or REPLY)
steps.detail: SEND/REPLY 801.5 ms (801.1 ms of it REPLY, the server holding its message) in 181 span(s) in a 1000 ms trace

steps.claim: Meanwhile the server rtdemo[21372930] 'S-server' is ready but not running, below the client's priority (no inheritance)
steps.detail: of the 801.5 ms wait the server was RUNNING (doing the work) for 400.2 ms; of the other 401.3 ms it was READY for 401.2 ms (100%), 401.2 ms of it below priority 30

steps.claim: A middle-priority thread holds the server's CPU
steps.detail: rtdemo[21360661] 'B-worker' (priority 20, 400.2 ms), devb-eide[90123] 'async_io' (priority 21, 0.0 ms) ran for 400.2 ms of the server's 401.2 ms READY time (100%)

steps.claim: Each wait for a reply ends while the server is running (it replies)
steps.detail: 100 of 100 completed REPLY waits ended while the server was RUNNING

limits: The trace does not name the server a client waits on (THSEND and THREPLY only name the waiting thread, and message events are not recorded); the server's identity comes from the snapshot.
The trace covers 1000 ms of the run; it shows what happened in that window only.
